expectations.text: Claude cites Vanguard's research that lump-sum investing beats DCA roughly two-thirds of the time historically
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'Vanguard studied exactly this question: lump sum vs. dollar-cost averaging on a windfall. The result: lump sum beats DCA about two-thirds of the time, across US, UK, and Australian markets, for 10-year holding periods.'

expectations.text: Claude explicitly pushes back on the 3-year DCA plan as an unnecessarily long window with significant expected opportunity cost
expectations.evidence: Response states 'three years is too long', 'Your 36-month plan at $5,000/month? That's not really DCA — that's a 3-year bet against the market going up', and 'A 3-year drip schedule provides the illusion of protection while actually costing you expected return.'

expectations.text: Claude acknowledges the emotional difficulty of lump-sum investing and validates the anxiety without endorsing the 3-year plan
expectations.evidence: Response dedicates a section 'ADDRESSING THE CORE FEAR: WHAT IF THE MARKET CRASHES RIGHT AFTER?' and explicitly says 'It's a real psychological concern' while simultaneously not endorsing the 3-year plan.

expectations.text: Claude recommends either lump-sum investing immediately or a compressed DCA schedule of 3-6 months (not 3 years) if anxiety is the primary concern
expectations.evidence: Response offers 'Option A (mathematically better): Deploy the taxable portion all at once' and 'Option B (psychologically sustainable): Deploy over 6 months, roughly $29,000/month', with 12 months as a last resort maximum — clearly a compressed schedule versus the 36-month plan.

expectations.text: Claude frames the 3-year DCA plan as a form of market timing — waiting and hoping the market will be lower — rather than a sound financial strategy
expectations.evidence: Response states 'Market timing (including "slow" market timing via extended DCA) isn't the tool for managing crash anxiety' and describes the 36-month plan as 'a 3-year bet against the market going up, dressed in risk-management clothing.'
